transcript.text: Good morning.
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: What can I do for you?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: I want to report a theft.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: I had some things stolen out of my bag yesterday.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: I’m sorry to hear that.
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: Right, so I’ll need to take a few details.
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: Can I start with your name?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: Louise Taylor.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: OK, thank you.
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: And are you resident in the UK?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: No, I’m actually Canadian.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: Though my mother was British.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: And your date of birth?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: December 14th, 1977.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: So you’re just visiting this country?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: I come over most summers on business.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: I’m an interior designer and I come over to buy old furniture, antiques you know.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: There are some really lovely things around here, but you need to get out to the small towns.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: I’ve had a really good trip this year, until this happened.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: So you’ve been here quite a while?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: Yes, I’m here for two months.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: I go back next week.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: So may I ask where you’re staying now?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: Well at present I’ve got a place at Park Apartments, that’s on King Street.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: I was staying at the Riverside Apartments on the same street, but the apartment there was only available for six weeks so I had to find another one.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: And the apartment number?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: Fifteen.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: Now, I need to take some details of the theft.
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: So you said you had some things stolen out of your bag?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: That’s right.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: And were you actually carrying the bag when the theft took place?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: Yes, I really can’t understand it.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: I had my backpack on.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: And I went into a supermarket to buy a few things and when I opened it up my wallet wasn’t there.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: And what did your wallet have in it?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: Well, fortunately I don’t keep my credit cards in that wallet – I keep them with my passport in an inside compartment in my backpack.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: But there was quite a bit of cash there … about £250 sterling, I should think.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: I withdrew £300 from my account yesterday, but I did a bit of shopping, so I must have already spent about £50 of that.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: At first I thought, oh I must have left the wallet back in the apartment, but then I realised my phone had gone as well.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: It was only a week old, and that’s when I realised I’d been robbed.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: Anyway at least they didn’t take the keys to my rental car.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: So you say the theft occurred yesterday?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: So that was September the tenth.
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: And do you have any idea at all of where or when the things might possibly have been stolen?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: Well at first I couldn’t believe it because the bag had been on my back ever since I left the apartment after lunch.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: It’s just a small backpack, but I generally use it when I’m travelling because it seems safer than a handbag.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: Anyway, I met up with a friend, and we spent a couple of hours in the museum.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: But I do remember that as we were leaving there, at about 4 o’clock, a group of young boys ran up to us, and they were really crowding round us, and they were asking us what time it was, then all of a sudden they ran off.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: Can you remember anything about them?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: The one who did most of the talking was wearing a T-shirt with a picture of something … let’s see … a tiger.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: Any idea of how old he might have been?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: Around twelve years old?
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: And can you remember anything else about his appearance?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: Not much.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: He was quite thin …
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: Colour of hair?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: I do remember that – he was blond.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: All the others were dark-haired.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: And any details of the others?
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: Not really.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: They came and went so quickly.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: So what I’m going to do now is give you a crime reference number so you can contact your insurance company.
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: So this is ten digits: 87954 82361.
transcript.speaker: OFFICER

transcript.text: Thank you.
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: So should I …
transcript.speaker: LOUISE

transcript.text: Good morning everyone.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: My name’s Janet Parker and I’m the human resources manager.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: We’re very happy to welcome you to your new apprenticeship.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I hope that the next six months will be a positive and enjoyable experience for you.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I’d like to start with some general advice about being an apprentice.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Most of you have very little or no experience of working for a big organisation and the first week or so may be quite challenging.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: There will be a lot of new information to take in but don’t worry too much about trying to remember everything.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: The important thing is to check with someone if you’re not sure what to do – you’ll find your supervisor is very approachable and won’t mind explaining things or helping you out. You’re here to learn so make the most of that opportunity. You’ll be spending time in different departments during your first week so make an effort to talk to as many people as possible about their work – you’ll make some new friends and find out lots of useful information.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: As well as having a supervisor, you’ll each be assigned a mentor.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This person will be someone who’s recently completed an apprenticeship and you’ll meet with them on a weekly basis.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Their role is to provide help and support throughout your apprenticeship.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Of course, this doesn’t mean they’ll actually do any of your work for you – instead they’ll be asking you about what goals you’ve achieved so far, as well as helping you to identify any areas for improvement. You can also discuss your more long-term ambitions with them as well.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Now I just want to run through a few company policies for our apprenticeship scheme with you… Most importantly, the internet.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: As part of your job you’ll be doing some research online so obviously you’ll have unlimited access for that but please don’t use it for personal use – you’ll have your own phones for that.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Some of you have already asked me about flexible working.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: After your probationary three-month period – some of you will be eligible for this – but it will depend on which department you’re in and what your personal circumstances are.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: So please don’t assume you’ll automatically be permitted to do this.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: I want to make sure there’s no confusion about our holiday policy.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Apart from any statutory public holidays we ask that you don’t book any holidays until after your six-month apprenticeship has finished.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Time off should only be taken if you are unwell.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Please speak to your supervisor if this is going to be a problem.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: You’ll be expected to work a 40-hour week but there may be opportunities to do overtime during busy periods.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Although you’re not required to do this, it can be a valuable experience – so we advise you to take it up if possible.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Obviously, we understand that people do have commitments outside work, so don’t worry if there are times when you are unavailable.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: As you know, we don’t have a formal dress code here – you may wear casual clothes as long as they’re practical – and the only restriction for shoes we have is on high heels for health and safety reasons.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Comfortable shoes like trainers are preferable.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: There’s a heavily subsidised canteen on site where you can get hot meals or salads cheaply.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: Snacks and drinks are also provided – so we’ve decided to introduce a no packed lunch policy.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: This is partly to encourage healthy eating at work and partly to stop people from eating at their workstation, which is unhygienic.
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: OK moving on to …
transcript.speaker: GUIDE

transcript.text: OK, so what I’d like you to do now is to talk to your partner about your presentations on urban planning.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: You should have done most of the reading now, so I’d like you to share your ideas, and talk about the structure of your presentation and what you need to do next.
transcript.speaker: TUTOR

transcript.text: OK Rob.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: I’m glad we chose quite a specific topic – cities built next to the sea.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: It made it much easier to find relevant information.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: And cities are growing so quickly – I mean, we know that more than half the world’s population lives in cities now.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Yeah, though that’s all cities, not just ones on the coast.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: But most of the biggest cities are actually built by the sea.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: I’d not realised that before.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: Nor me.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: And what’s more, a lot of them are built at places where rivers come out into the sea.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: But apparently this can be a problem.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Why?
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: Well, as the city expands, agriculture and industry tend to spread further inland along the rivers, and so agriculture moves even further inland up the river.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: That’s not necessarily a problem, except it means more and more pollutants are discharged into the rivers.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: So these are brought downstream to the cities?
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Hmm.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Did you read that article about Miami, on the east coast of the USA?
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: No.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: Well, apparently back in the 1950s they built channels to drain away the water in case of flooding.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Sounds sensible.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: Yeah, they spent quite a lot of money on them.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: But what they didn’t take into account was global warming.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: So they built the drainage channels too close to sea level, and now sea levels are rising, they’re more or less useless.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: If there’s a lot of rain, the water can’t run away, there’s nowhere for it to go.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: The whole design was faulty.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: So what are the authorities doing about it now?
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: I don’t know.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: I did read that they’re aiming to stop disposing of waste into the ocean over the next ten years.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: But that won’t help with flood prevention now, will it?
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: No.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Really they just need to find the money for something to replace the drainage channels, in order to protect against flooding now.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: But in the long term they need to consider the whole ecosystem.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Right.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: Really, though, coastal cities can’t deal with their problems on their own, can they?
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: I mean, they’ve got to start acting together at an international level instead of just doing their own thing.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: Absolutely.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: The thing is, everyone knows what the problems are and environmentalists have a pretty good idea of what we should be doing about them, so they should be able to work together to some extent.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: But it’s going to be a long time before countries come to a decision on what principles they’re prepared to abide by.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Yes, if they ever do.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: So I think we’ve probably got enough for our presentation.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: It’s only fifteen minutes.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: So I suppose we’ll begin with some general historical background about why coastal cities were established.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: But we don’t want to spend too long on that, the other students will already know a bit about it.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: It’s all to do with communications and so on.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Yes.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: We should mention some geographical factors, things like wetlands and river estuaries and coastal erosion and so on.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: We could have some maps of different cities with these features marked.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: On a handout you mean?
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Or some slides everyone can see?
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Yeah, that’d be better.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: It’d be good to go into past mistakes in a bit more detail.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Did you read that case study of the problems there were in New Orleans with flooding a few years ago?
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Yes, We could use that as the basis for that part of the talk.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: I don’t think the other students will have read it, but they’ll remember hearing about the flooding at the time.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: So that’s probably enough background.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: So then we’ll go on to talk about what action’s being taken to deal with the problems of coastal cities.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: What else do we need to talk about?
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Maybe something on future risks, looking more at the long term, if populations continue to grow.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Yeah.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: We’ll need to do a bit of work there, I haven’t got much information, have you?
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: No.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: We’ll need to look at some websites.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Shouldn’t take too long.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: OK.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: And I think we should end by talking about international implications.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: Maybe we could ask people in the audience.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: We’ve got people from quite a lot of different places.
transcript.speaker: CARLA

transcript.text: That’d be interesting, if we have time, yes.
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: So now shall we …
transcript.speaker: ROB

transcript.text: Producing enough energy to meet our needs has become a serious problem.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Demand is rising rapidly, because of the world’s increasing population and expanding industry.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Burning fossil fuels, like gas, coal and oil, seriously damages the environment and they’ll eventually run out.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For a number of years now, scientists have been working out how we can derive energy from renewable sources, such as the sun and wind, without causing pollution.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Today I’ll outline marine renewable energy – also called ocean energy – which harnesses the movement of the oceans.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Marine renewable energy can be divided into three main categories: wave energy, tidal energy and ocean thermal energy conversion, and I’ll say a few words about each one.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: First, wave energy.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Numerous devices have been invented to harvest wave energy, with names such as Wave Dragon, the Penguin and Mighty Whale, and research is going on to try and come up with a really efficient method.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This form of energy has plenty of potential, as the source is constant, and there’s no danger of waves coming to s standstill.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Electricity can be generated using onshore systems, using a reservoir, or offshore systems.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But the problem with ocean waves is that they’re erratic, with the wind making them travel in every direction.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This adds to the difficulty of creating efficient technology: ideally all the waves would travel smoothly and regularly along the same straight line.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Another drawback is that sand and other sediment on the ocean floor might be stopped from flowing normally, which can lead to environmental problems.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The second category of marine energy that I’ll mention is tidal energy.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: One major advantage of using the tide, rather than waves, as a source of energy is that it’s predictable: we know the exact time of high and low tides for years to come.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: For tidal energy to be effective, the difference between high and low tides needs to be at least five metres, and this occurs naturally in only about forty places on Earth.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: But the right conditions can be created by constructing a tidal lagoon, an area of sea water separated from the sea.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: One current plan is to create a tidal lagoon on the coast of Wales.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This will be an area of water within a bay at Swansea, sheltered by a U-shaped breakwater, or dam, built out from the coast.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The breakwater will contain sixteen hydro turbines, and as the tide rises, water rushes through the breakwater, activating the turbines, which turn a generator to produce electricity.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Then, for three hours as the tide goes out, the water is held back within the breakwater, increasing the difference in water level, until it’s several metres higher within the lagoon than in the open sea.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: Then, in order to release the stored water, gates in the breakwater are opened.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It pours powerfully out of the lagoon, driving the turbines in the breakwater in the opposite direction and again generating thousands of megawatts of electricity.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: As there are two high tides a day, this lagoon scheme would generate electricity four times a day, every day, for a total of around 14 hours in every 24 – and enough electricity for over 150,000 homes.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This system has quite a lot in its favour: unlike solar and wind energy it doesn’t depend on the weather; the turbines are operated without the need for fuel, so it doesn’t create any greenhouse gas emissions; and very little maintenance is needed.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: It’s estimated that electricity generated in this way will be relatively cheap, and that manufacturing the components would create than 2,000 jobs, a big boost to the local economy.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: On the other hand, there are fears that lagoons might harm both fish and birds, for example by disturbing migration patterns, and causing a build-up of silt, affecting local ecosystems.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: There are other forms of tidal energy, but I’ll go on to the third category of marine energy: ocean thermal energy conversion.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: This depends on there being a big difference in temperature between surface water and the water a couple of kilometres below the surface, and this occurs in tropical coastal areas.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The idea is to bring cold water up to the surface using a submerged pipe.
transcript.speaker: LECTURER

transcript.text: The concept dates back to 1881, when …
transcript.speaker: LECTURER
